newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls for peaceful settlement in Sudan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls for peaceful settlement in Sudan.

text.p: The United States Tuesday called on all parties involved in fighting in eastern Sudan to settle their differences peacefully, but declined comment on whether foreign countries were involved.

"The United States is concerned by the recent fighting," the U.S. State Department said. "We are urging on all, on the Sudanese government, on the rebels and anyone else involved in this fighting restraint and a peaceful resolution of any differences here."
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had contacted the warring parties to urge them to avoid harming civilians and to treat all prisoners of war according to international conventions.
The fighting began nine days ago with an offensive by the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA).

Sudan's President Omar Hassan al-Bashir has said Ethiopian and Eritrean troops, with some help from Israel, are behind the fighting. Eritrea and Ethiopia, which allow Sudanese opposition groups to operate on their territory, deny being involved.
"I can't comment on the role that other countries may or may not be playing," Burns told a news briefing.

But Burns denied that U.S. aid could have contributed to the conflict. Washington had not extended any lethal military assistance to Sudan's neighbours Ethiopia, Uganda and Eritrea, while non-lethal assistance of some $15 million in the 1996 budget had not so far reached those countries, he said.
He also dismissed suggestions that Israel was involved in the conflict.
The United States has poor relations with Sudan, a country it has placed on its list of states alleged to sponsor terrorism.
Burns said Washington believed the Organisation of African Unity and not the U.N. Security Council was the body best able to seek to resolve the situation in eastern Sudan.
